knowledge_statements.title: Interior-State Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interior-point reoptimization initialized from a repaired primal-dual state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a modified relaxation, start from a stored primal-dual state \((x,y,z)\). Map it to the new variables and constraints, then repair positivity and numerical interiority, for example by replacing required positive components with values at least \(\delta>0\). Recompute residuals for the modified problem and apply the chosen interior-point iterations with their usual neighborhood, merit, and stopping rules. If the repaired state is inadmissible or residuals are unacceptable, discard it and use the solver's default initialization. Return a solution and bound only when the ordinary termination tests certify them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Map and repair a stored primal-dual interior state, reject it when unsuitable, and retain the solver’s ordinary validity and stopping tests.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation solver admits a primal-dual interior-point initialization.
The stored state can be mapped to the modified problem's variables and constraints.

children.title: Warm-Start Degradation

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which a reused relaxation state provides little benefit or increases solution effort.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W(R,R',s)\) denote the work required to solve modified relaxation \(R'\) from a state \(s\) obtained for \(R\), and let \(W_0(R')\) denote work under default initialization. No general monotonic improvement guarantee holds: large bound changes, added or deleted constraints, loss of primal or dual feasibility, ill-conditioning, or expensive state repair can yield \(W(R,R',s)\ge W_0(R')\). Therefore a warm start is an efficiency heuristic unless a solver-specific complexity result applies. Correctness requires detecting incompatible states and retaining the same feasibility, optimality, and bound-validation tests used for a cold start.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Major model changes or poor compatibility can erase warm-start gains or make reuse slower; correctness still relies on ordinary solver certificates.
assumptions_latex: Both runs solve the same modified relaxation \(R'\) to the same termination tolerances.
Work includes state repair and all subsequent solver iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is generally no guarantee that \(W(R,R',s)<W_0(R')\).

solver-specific empirical or complexity evidence is required

children.title: Large Relaxation-Gap Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Large Relaxation-Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branch-and-bound regimes in which relaxation bounds remain far from feasible incumbent values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization node \(v\), let \(L_v\) be a valid relaxation lower bound and let \(U\) be the incumbent value. Define the absolute node gap \(G_v=U-L_v\) for \(L_v\le U\). A large relaxation-gap regime is one in which \(G_v\) remains above the pruning tolerance for many frontier nodes, so the bound test \(L_v\ge U-\varepsilon\) rarely closes nodes. Weak bounds alone do not imply a universal tree-size lower bound, because branching, propagation, heuristics, and structure may still resolve nodes; they identify failure of bound-based discrimination rather than inevitable exponential search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistently large incumbent-to-relaxation gaps prevent most bound pruning, though they do not alone prove that the search tree must be large.
assumptions_latex: The problem is minimized and \(U\) is the value of a feasible incumbent.
Each \(L_v\) is a valid node lower bound and \(\varepsilon\ge0\) is the pruning tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_v>\varepsilon\) implies that node \(v\) cannot be closed by the test \(L_v\ge U-\varepsilon\).

children.title: Low-Discrimination Frontier Regimes

children.title: Bound Plateaus
children.top_down_role: Search regions where successive nodes show little objective-bound improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound Plateaus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines near-equality of node bounds on a minimization branch-and-bound frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a nonempty finite set of active branch-and-bound nodes, and let \(L(v)\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\) be the valid lower bound at node \(v\). For a finite tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge 0\), the frontier is an \(\varepsilon\)-bound plateau when every bound is finite and \[\max_{v\in A}L(v)-\min_{v\in A}L(v)\le \varepsilon.\] An exact bound plateau is the case \(\varepsilon=0\). On such a plateau, any node-selection rule depending only on \(L(v)\) cannot strictly rank nodes whose bounds coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound plateau occurs when all active-node lower bounds lie within a prescribed tolerance, so bound-only node selection provides little or no discrimination.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is finite and nonempty.
\(L(v)\) is a finite valid lower bound for every \(v\in A\).
\(\varepsilon\ge 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{v\in A}L(v)-\min_{v\in A}L(v)\le\varepsilon\), with exact equality of all bounds when \(\varepsilon=0\).

children.title: Degenerate Frontiers
children.top_down_role: Active-node populations with extensive bound ties or near-ties.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Frontiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses bound-based indistinguishability as the local meaning of frontier degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be the active-node frontier and let \(s:A\to\mathbb{R}^q\) collect every numerical component used by a node-selection rule before its final tie-breaker. The frontier is selection-degenerate on a subset \(T\subseteq A\) when \(|T|\ge2\) and \(s(u)=s(v)\) for all \(u,v\in T\). It is fully degenerate when this holds with \(T=A\). Consequently, the stated selection components cannot distinguish nodes in \(T\); their order is determined only by an external tie-breaking convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A frontier is degenerate when two or more active nodes have identical values for every score component used before tie-breaking.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite active-node set.
\(s\) contains all pre-tie-break selection scores.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For all \(u,v\in T\), \(s(u)=s(v)\), so the score rule induces a tie throughout \(T\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is coherent and definition is an appropriate content kind, but selection degeneracy defined through equality of an arbitrary vector of pre-tie-break scores is a local convention. No source establishes this exact meaning of Degenerate Frontiers.

children.title: Low-Discrimination Node Pools
children.top_down_role: Frontiers offering weak bound-based separation among node choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Discrimination Node Pools
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies weak separation of active nodes under a scalar selection score.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a nonempty finite pool of active nodes and let \(s:P\to\mathbb{R}\) be a score to be minimized. For tolerance \(\delta\ge0\), the pool has \(\delta\)-low discrimination when \[\max_{v\in P}s(v)-\min_{v\in P}s(v)\le\delta.\] More generally, for a vector score \(s:P\to\mathbb{R}^q\) with component tolerances \(\delta_i\ge0\), low discrimination means \(\max_{v\in P}s_i(v)-\min_{v\in P}s_i(v)\le\delta_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node pool has low discrimination when the range of each selection score across the pool is no larger than its chosen tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is finite and nonempty.
Each score component is real-valued on \(P\).
All tolerances are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every designated selection-score range over \(P\) is bounded by its corresponding tolerance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar and componentwise range conditions are mathematically well-defined and condition is suitable for this leaf. The designation low discrimination and its absolute-tolerance convention are nevertheless unsupported by a cited source.

children.title: Plateau-Induced Tree Growth
children.top_down_role: Expansion pressure caused by prolonged lack of bound differentiation.

knowledge_statements.title: Plateau-Induced Tree Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts nodes when equal bounds prevent pruning throughout a regular branching subtree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimization branch-and-bound subtree rooted at depth zero. Suppose every processed node of depth less than \(d\) generates exactly \(b\ge2\) children, all generated nodes remain feasible, and no node through depth \(d\) is pruned by bounds, integrality, or dominance. If plateaued bounds force exploration of every such node, then the number of generated nodes through depth \(d\) is \[N_d=\sum_{i=0}^{d}b^i=\frac{b^{d+1}-1}{b-1}.\] Hence \(N_d\in\Theta(b^d)\), measured in generated branch-and-bound nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a bound plateau prevents pruning in a full branching subtree, the generated-node count grows geometrically and is exponential in depth.
assumptions_latex: Every internal node through depth \(d-1\) has exactly \(b\ge2\) children.
No generated node through depth \(d\) is otherwise pruned.
All nodes through depth \(d\) must be explored.

children.title: Unsafe-Bound Pruning Failures
children.top_down_role: Incorrect subtree closure caused by invalid or misqualified bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Unsafe-Bound Pruning Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite minimization example showing loss of the optimum under an invalid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize \(f(x)\) over \(x\in\{0,1\}\), where \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(1)=10\). Suppose \(x=1\) supplies incumbent value \(U=10\). At the node fixing \(x=0\), let an invalid procedure report the claimed lower bound \(\widehat L=11\). The usual minimization test \(\widehat L\ge U\) prunes this node, although its true subtree optimum is \(L^*=0<U\). The algorithm consequently returns value \(10\) and discards the global optimizer \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An overestimated subtree lower bound can satisfy the pruning test while hiding a better feasible solution, causing an incorrect final answer.
assumptions_latex: The problem is minimized over \(\{0,1\}\).
The incumbent value is \(U=10\).
The reported node bound \(\widehat L=11\) is not valid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pruning from \(\widehat L\ge U\) removes the optimizer because the true node optimum satisfies \(L^*=0<U\).

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Optimality Condition via Bounds p. 14

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Optimality Condition via Bounds p. 14

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unsafe pruning caused by applying a lower-bound certificate outside the node, model, objective, or approximation scope for which it was established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a current minimization node with feasible set \(X_v\), objective \(f\), and incumbent value \(U\), a reported value \(\widehat L\) can justify pruning by \(\widehat L\ge U\) only if its certificate entails \(\widehat L\le\inf_{x\in X_v}f(x)\). A certificate only for a strict restriction \(Y\subsetneq X_v\), a different objective, a different model version, or an uncertified approximate solve does not generally entail this inequality. A previously certified bound remains safe after a change only when its validity for the current node optimum is preserved; for example, a lower bound for a superset remains valid after feasible-set restriction when the objective is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerically plausible bound is unsafe for pruning when its certificate does not cover the current node, model, and objective; stale bounds remain usable only when their original validity implication survives the change.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is the value of a feasible incumbent for the current minimization model.
Pruning is proposed from \(\widehat L\ge U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a certificate implying \(\widehat L\le\inf_{x\in X_v}f(x)\), the comparison \(\widehat L\ge U\) is not a valid subtree-closure certificate.

notation.meaning: current feasible set represented by node v

children.title: Single-Variable Branching
children.top_down_role: Partitions generated by selecting one variable as the branching object.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Variable Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard binary branching on a fractional integer-constrained coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a branch-and-bound node, solve the relaxation and obtain \(\bar x\). Choose an integer-constrained coordinate \(j\) with \(\bar x_j\notin\mathbb Z\). Create two children by adding, respectively, \[x_j\le\lfloor\bar x_j\rfloor\qquad\text{and}\qquad x_j\ge\lceil\bar x_j\rceil.\] Each integer-feasible point of the parent satisfies at least one child constraint, while \(\bar x\) satisfies neither. Continue processing the children under the usual pruning rules; stop when no active node remains and return the best certified incumbent, or infeasibility if none exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on one fractional integer variable by creating floor and ceiling children, which cover every integer-feasible parent solution but exclude the fractional relaxation point.
assumptions_latex: \(j\) indexes an integer-constrained variable.
\(\bar x_j\notin\mathbb Z\).
The parent relaxation has been solved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two children cover all integer-feasible parent points and exclude \(\bar x\).

children.title: Discrete-Domain Branching
children.top_down_role: Partitions formed from subsets or intervals of a discrete variable domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Domain Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact branching by partitioning one variable's finite discrete domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let variable \(x_j\) have current finite domain \(D\). Choose nonempty pairwise disjoint sets \(D_1,\ldots,D_m\) satisfying \(D=\bigcup_{r=1}^mD_r\), with \(m\ge2\). Create child \(r\) by imposing \(x_j\in D_r\) together with all parent constraints. The child feasible sets are pairwise disjoint and their union equals the parent's feasible set. Process these children under the chosen node-selection and pruning rules, and return the best certified incumbent after the active pool is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition a finite variable domain into disjoint nonempty subsets and create one child per subset, preserving an exact partition of parent solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is the current finite domain of \(x_j\).
\(D_1,\ldots,D_m\) form a nonempty disjoint partition of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The child feasible regions are disjoint and their union is the parent feasible region.

notation.meaning: domain subset assigned to child r

children.title: Bound-Change Branching
children.top_down_role: Child regions represented through local variable-bound changes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate branching represented solely by complementary child-specific bound tightenings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an integer variable has current bounds \(\ell_j\le x_j\le u_j\), and choose an integer threshold \(t\) with \(\ell_j\le t<u_j\). Create a left child by replacing \(u_j\) with \(t\), and a right child by replacing \(\ell_j\) with \(t+1\), leaving all other parent restrictions unchanged. For integer \(x_j\), the alternatives \(x_j\le t\) and \(x_j\ge t+1\) are disjoint and exhaustive. A child whose propagated lower bound exceeds its upper bound is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tighten one child's upper bound and the other's lower bound at consecutive integers, exactly partitioning the selected integer coordinate range.
assumptions_latex: \(x_j\) is integer constrained.
\(\ell_j,t,u_j\in\mathbb Z\) and \(\ell_j\le t<u_j\).
All other parent restrictions are inherited unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x_j\in\mathbb Z:\ell_j\le x_j\le u_j\}=\{x_j:\ell_j\le x_j\le t\}\mathbin{\dot\cup}\{x_j:t+1\le x_j\le u_j\}.

notation.meaning: Current lower bound of the selected variable.
Current upper bound of the selected variable.

children.title: General Split Branching
children.top_down_role: Branching based on general integral split disjunctions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Branching use of a two-term split on a nonzero integral linear form of integer-constrained variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) index integer-constrained variables, \(\pi\in\mathbb Z^I\setminus\{0\}\), \(\pi_0\in\mathbb Z\), and let \(P\) be the parent region. Create \(P^-=P\cap\{x:\pi^\top x_I\le \pi_0\}\) and \(P^+=P\cap\{x:\pi^\top x_I\ge \pi_0+1\}\). Every mixed-integer-feasible point of \(P\) lies in exactly one child, while every point satisfying \(\pi_0<\pi^\top x_I<\pi_0+1\) is excluded from both children.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branch on a nonzero integer linear form at consecutive integer levels; the two children partition all mixed-integer-feasible parent points and exclude the intervening open slab.
assumptions_latex: \(x_I\in\mathbb Z^I\) at mixed-integer-feasible points.
\(\pi\in\mathbb Z^I\setminus\{0\}\).
\(\pi_0\in\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P^-\mathbin{\dot\cup}P^+\text{ contains every mixed-integer-feasible point of }P.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Form Split Branching
General Split Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Split disjunction on an integral linear form of integer-constrained variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) index integer-constrained variables, let \(\pi\in\mathbb Z^{I}\setminus\{0\}\), and let \(\pi_0\in\mathbb Z\). General split branching replaces a parent region \(P\) by the two children \[P^- = P\cap\{x:\pi^\top x_I\le\pi_0\},\qquad P^+ = P\cap\{x:\pi^\top x_I\ge\pi_0+1\}.\] Because \(\pi^\top x_I\in\mathbb Z\) for every mixed-integer-feasible point, every such point in \(P\) belongs to at least one child, and the two children are disjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general split branches on an integer linear form, using consecutive integer thresholds that disjointly cover all mixed-integer-feasible parent points.
assumptions_latex: \(x_I\in\mathbb Z^{I}\) at mixed-integer-feasible points.
\(\pi\in\mathbb Z^{I}\setminus\{0\}\).
\(\pi_0\in\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^-\) and \(P^+\) are disjoint and cover every mixed-integer-feasible point of \(P\).

children.title: Multivariable Branching
children.top_down_role: Disjunctions whose alternatives involve multiple variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite valid branching disjunctions whose predicates jointly involve multiple coordinates, excluding the separately treated integral-split family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|J|\ge2\), let \(P\) be a parent region, and let \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_m\) be finitely many sets described in the joint coordinates \(x_J\). They define a valid multivariable branch when every mixed-integer-feasible point of \(P\) lies in \(\bigcup_{r=1}^m Q_r\); child \(r\) is \(P_r=P\cap Q_r\). Pairwise disjointness on the mixed-integer-feasible set makes the children a partition, whereas coverage alone permits overlapping children.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multivariable branch creates children from a finite valid disjunction formulated jointly in at least two coordinates; alternatives may cover or, when disjoint, partition the feasible parent points.
assumptions_latex: The family \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_m\) is finite.
Every mixed-integer-feasible point of \(P\) belongs to at least one \(Q_r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\cap X_{MI}\subseteq\bigcup_{r=1}^m(P_r\cap X_{MI}).
knowledge_statements.title: Multivariable Disjunctive Branching
Multivariable Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite disjunctive branching whose alternatives jointly depend on several variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a parent region \(P\), choose sets \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_m\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) with \(m\ge2\) such that every mixed-integer-feasible point of \(P\) belongs to \(\bigcup_{r=1}^mQ_r\), and each \(Q_r\) is described using at least two selected coordinates. Create child regions \(P_r=P\cap Q_r\), discard empty children, and process the remainder under the usual bounding and pruning rules. If the \(Q_r\) are pairwise disjoint on the mixed-integer lattice, the children form a partition; otherwise they form a covering branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Create children from a finite disjunction involving multiple coordinates, requiring the alternatives to cover every mixed-integer-feasible parent point.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is the current parent region.
The finite family \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_m\) covers all mixed-integer-feasible points of \(P\).
Each alternative depends on at least two selected coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every mixed-integer-feasible parent point lies in at least one child \(P_r=P\cap Q_r\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction is internally consistent and algorithm fits the leaf, but the definition of multivariable branching through arbitrary covering sets, including the requirement that each set use at least two coordinates and the allowance of overlapping children, is convention-dependent. An authoritative source for this exact branching-family scope is required.

children.title: Split-Geometry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric forms of non-coordinate-aligned search-space partitions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relaxation Geometry of an Integral Split
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-contained geometry of a relaxation relative to the two split half-spaces and their intervening open slab.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(\pi\in\mathbb Z^I\setminus\{0\}\), and \(\pi_0\in\mathbb Z\), define \(P^-=P\cap\{x:\pi^\top x_I\le\pi_0\}\), \(P^+=P\cap\{x:\pi^\top x_I\ge\pi_0+1\}\), and \(S=\{x:\pi_0<\pi^\top x_I<\pi_0+1\}\). Exactly one of four child-incidence regimes holds: both children are empty, only \(P^-\) is nonempty, only \(P^+\) is nonempty, or both are nonempty. Moreover, \(P\setminus(P^-\cup P^+)=P\cap S\), so the split removes relaxation points exactly when \(P\cap S\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation can meet neither, one, or both split half-spaces; the relaxation points removed by the split are exactly those in the intervening open slab.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
\(\pi\in\mathbb Z^I\setminus\{0\}\).
\(\pi_0\in\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\setminus(P^-\cup P^+)=P\cap S.

notation.meaning: intersections of the relaxation with the two split half-spaces
open slab between consecutive split levels

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Geometry of an Integral Split
Split-Geometry Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies how a relaxation intersects the two half-spaces and excluded split slab.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a relaxation \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and split \((\pi,\pi_0)\), define \(P^-\), \(P^+\) as the two split children and define the open slab \(S=\{x:\pi_0<\pi^\top x_I<\pi_0+1\}\). The split geometry has four exhaustive intersection regimes: both children empty; only \(P^-\) nonempty; only \(P^+\) nonempty; or both children nonempty. The split cuts the current relaxation precisely when \(P\cap S\ne\varnothing\). It changes neither child geometry when \(P\cap S=\varnothing\), because then \(P=P^-\cup P^+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split geometry is determined by which child half-spaces intersect the relaxation and whether the relaxation enters the open slab between them.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
\(\pi\in\mathbb Z^{I}\setminus\{0\}\) and \(\pi_0\in\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four child-emptiness regimes are exhaustive, and the split removes relaxation points exactly when \(P\cap S\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: open slab excluded by the split disjunction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate kind for this geometric classification, and the four child-emptiness cases and slab-removal criterion are mathematically consistent when the standard split-child definitions are imported. However, those child formulas are not restated locally and no source supports the proposed four-regime taxonomy or terminology.

children.title: Multivariable Partition Complexity
children.top_down_role: Representation and evaluation burdens associated with multivariable alternatives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Child-count and regular-tree growth for simultaneous Cartesian partitions of several discrete domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If selected discrete variable \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) is partitioned into \(m_i\ge2\) nonempty pieces and every Cartesian product of pieces generates a child, then the pre-filtering branching factor is \(B=\prod_{i=1}^k m_i\). If every internal node has this branching factor through depth \(d\) and no child is pruned, the total generated-node count is \(N_d=\sum_{r=0}^dB^r=(B^{d+1}-1)/(B-1)\in\Theta(B^d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous Cartesian domain partitioning creates the product of the piece counts as children and yields geometric node growth in a complete unpruned regular tree.
assumptions_latex: Each of \(k\) selected discrete domains is independently partitioned into \(m_i\ge2\) nonempty pieces.
One child is generated for every Cartesian product of pieces.
For the depth bound, the same branching factor applies at every internal node and no child is pruned.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B=\prod_{i=1}^k m_i,\qquad N_d=\frac{B^{d+1}-1}{B-1}\in\Theta(B^d).

notation.meaning: number of pieces for selected domain i

knowledge_statements.title: Cartesian Partition Branching Factor
Multivariable Partition Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts children and regular-tree nodes for Cartesian multivariable domain branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select \(k\) discrete variables. If variable \(i\) is partitioned into \(m_i\ge2\) nonempty domain pieces and one child is created for every Cartesian product of pieces, then a single multivariable branching operation creates \[B=\prod_{i=1}^{k}m_i\] children before infeasibility filtering. If the same complete partition occurs at every internal node for \(d\) levels and no child is pruned, the generated-node count is \[N_d=\sum_{r=0}^{d}B^r=\frac{B^{d+1}-1}{B-1}\in\Theta(B^d).\] The resource measured is generated branch-and-bound nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cartesian branching on several partitioned domains creates the product of their piece counts as children, producing geometric tree growth without pruning.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) discrete variables are partitioned independently.
Variable \(i\) has \(m_i\ge2\) nonempty pieces.
No generated child is pruned in the depth-\(d\) regular-tree model.

notation.meaning: number of domain pieces for selected variable i

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_1=[0,1]\) and \(F_2=[1/2,3/2]\). Then \(F=F_1\cup F_2=[0,3/2]\), but every point in \([1/2,1]\) belongs to both alternatives. A branching rule whose children are exactly \(F_1\) and \(F_2\) preserves feasibility because their union is \(F\), yet it does not create disjoint child regions. Consequently, any search-size or measure argument that sums child contributions as though \(F_1\mathbin{\dot\cup}F_2=F\) is invalid unless alternatives are disambiguated by state variables or duplicate membership is otherwise controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overlapping alternatives preserve coverage but duplicate feasible points across children, invalidating bounds that require a disjoint partition.

children.title: Special-Ordered-Set Branching

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary branching on a nonnegative SOS1 variable family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\ge0\) satisfy the SOS1 restriction that at most one component is positive. For a nontrivial partition \(\{1,\ldots,m\}=L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\), create one child with \(x_i=0\) for all \(i\in L\) and the other with \(x_i=0\) for all \(i\in R\). Their union contains every SOS1-feasible point; their intersection consists of points with every SOS1 component zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split the SOS1 indices into two blocks and force one block to zero in each child; the children cover the set and overlap only at the all-zero SOS state.

\(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R=\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with both blocks nonempty.

Create a left child by fixing \(x_j=0\) for \(j\ge k+2\), and a right child by fixing \(x_j=0\) for \(j\le k-1\). The children cover every SOS2-feasible point; each child restricts possible positive support to its corresponding ordered range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split an SOS2 ordering into two overlapping ranges and fix variables outside the selected range to zero in each child.

They form an SOS1 set: at most one \(x_i\) may be positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For any nontrivial index partition \(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), the disjunction \(\sum_{i\in L}x_i=0\) or \(\sum_{i\in R}x_i=0\) covers every SOS1-feasible point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary SOS1 branching; SOS2 geometry is treated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an SOS1 set \((x_1,ldots,x_m)\), choose nonempty blocks \(L\) and \(R\) with \(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R=\{1,ldots,m\}\). Create a left child imposing \(x_i=0\) for every \(i\in L\), and a right child imposing \(x_i=0\) for every \(i\in R\). Apply bound and feasibility tests to each child and stop when the active SOS member is determined or the node is pruned. Since an SOS1-feasible point has at most one positive component, it satisfies at least one child; the all-zero point satisfies both.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) for \(i\in G\) and \(\sum_{i\in G}x_i\le1\). Choose a nontrivial partition \(G=L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\). Form one child by imposing \(\sum_{i\in L}x_i=0\), and the other by imposing \(\sum_{i\in R}x_i=0\). Continue bounding or branching within each child and prune by infeasibility or incumbent dominance. Because at most one group variable equals one, every GUB-feasible vector satisfies at least one child; the vector with all group variables zero belongs to both.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition a binary GUB group and force one side to zero in each child; every feasible group assignment is retained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Disjointness Criterion for a GUB Split
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact overlap criterion for the two zero-block children of binary GUB branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\{x\in\{0,1\}^{G}:\sum_{i\in G}x_i\le 1\}\), let \(G=L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\), and define \(F_L=F\cap\{x_i=0\ (i\in L)\}\) and \(F_R=F\cap\{x_i=0\ (i\in R)\}\). Then \(F_L\cap F_R=F\cap\{x_i=0\ (i\in G)\}\). Hence the children are disjoint exactly when the all-zero group state is infeasible in \(F\); in particular, \(\sum_{i\in G}x_i=1\) is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two GUB children overlap exactly on parent-feasible assignments with every group variable zero; exact-one selection makes them disjoint.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\{x\in\{0,1\}^{G}:\sum_{i\in G}x_i\le1\}\).
\(G=L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\) with \(L,R\ne\varnothing\).

children.title: Ordered-Set Partition Geometry
children.top_down_role: Child-region organization induced by an ordering over set members.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set geometry induced by splitting an SOS2 ordering at one adjacent boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the set of nonnegative vectors \(x\in\mathbb{R}^m\) whose positive support is contained in \(\{i,i+1\}\) for some \(i\). For \(k\in\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\), set \(S_L=S\cap\{x_j=0\text{ for }j\ge k+2\}\) and \(S_R=S\cap\{x_j=0\text{ for }j\le k-1\}\). Then \(S=S_L\cup S_R\) and \(S_L\cap S_R=S\cap\{x_j=0\text{ for }j\notin\{k,k+1\}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two overlapping ordered ranges cover an SOS2 set, and their intersection is exactly the feasible support confined to the boundary pair.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^m_+\).
The positive support of every \(x\in S\) lies in one adjacent index pair.

knowledge_statements.title: SOS2 Boundary-Overlap Geometry

assumptions_latex: The ordered nonnegative variables \((x_1,ldots,x_m)\) satisfy SOS2: positive components have indices in some pair \(\{i,i+1\}\).
A split index \(k\in\{1,ldots,m-1\}\) is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two restricted SOS2 sets cover the parent, and their intersection has support contained in \(\{k,k+1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support geometry of a binary split of an SOS2 set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the SOS2-feasible set and fix \(k\in\{1,ldots,m-1\}\). Define \(S_L=S\cap\{x:x_j=0\text{ for }j\ge k+2\}\) and \(S_R=S\cap\{x:x_j=0\text{ for }j\le k-1\}\). Every support contained in an adjacent pair lies wholly within \(\{1,ldots,k+1\}\) or within \(\{k,ldots,m\}\), so \(S=S_L\cup S_R\). Moreover, \(S_L\cap S_R\) consists only of points whose support is contained in the boundary pair \(\{k,k+1\}\); thus ordered branching localizes, but does not necessarily eliminate, child overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS2 split uses two overlapping ordered index ranges whose intersection is confined to the boundary pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordered-Set Partition Geometry

children.title: Group-Structure Degradation
children.top_down_role: Regimes where weak or disrupted group structure limits branching effectiveness.

knowledge_statements.title: Group-Structure Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of GUB or SOS support restrictions destroys branching coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\), suppose \(x_i\ge 0\) for every \(i\in G\), and suppose the parent feasible set contains a point \(x^*\) with \(x_p^*>0\) for some \(p\in L\) and \(x_q^*>0\) for some \(q\in R\). Then \(\sum_{i\in L}x_i^*>0\) and \(\sum_{i\in R}x_i^*>0\), so \(x^*\) satisfies neither proposed child constraint \(\sum_{i\in L}x_i=0\) nor \(\sum_{i\in R}x_i=0\). Hence this group-branching disjunction is invalid unless the model forbids simultaneous activity across the two blocks, as an SOS1 or binary GUB restriction does. If that structure is absent or incorrectly detected, branching can delete feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative group variables, if a feasible point can activate variables on both sides of the split, forcing one side to zero in each child removes that point and makes the branching disjunction invalid.
assumptions_latex: The proposed group split is \(G=L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\), and \(x_i\ge0\) for every \(i\in G\).
The parent feasible set contains a point with a positive component indexed by \(L\) and a positive component indexed by \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The disjunction \(\sum_{i\in L}x_i=0\) or \(\sum_{i\in R}x_i=0\) is not valid for the parent feasible set.

notation.meaning: Two blocks of the proposed group
A parent-feasible point active in both blocks

children.title: Spatial Branching
children.top_down_role: Subdivision of continuous nonconvex domains using spatial decisions.

assumptions_latex: The current continuous domain is a box \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\).
A coordinate \(j\) with \(\ell_j<u_j\) and split point \(s\in(\ell_j,u_j)\) are selected.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\), choose \(j\) with \(\ell_j<u_j\) and \(s\in(\ell_j,u_j)\). Create \(B^- =B\cap\{x:x_j\le s\}\) and \(B^+=B\cap\{x:x_j\ge s\}\). Construct the prescribed relaxation and lower bound on each child, prune infeasible or dominated children, and otherwise repeat. The children satisfy \(B=B^-\cup B^+\), their interiors are disjoint, and their common boundary is \(B\cap\{x:x_j=s\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split one interval of the current box at an interior point, then bound and process the two resulting subboxes.

assumptions_latex: A root box \(B^0\subset\mathbb R^n\) is repeatedly split by coordinate hyperplanes.
Each split point lies in the interior of the selected coordinate interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At every finite depth, the leaf boxes cover \(B^0\), have pairwise disjoint interiors, and their volumes sum to \(\operatorname{vol}(B^0)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite geometric partition induced by recursive coordinate splits.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Cuts, Lower Bounds and Box Reduction p. 83
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L\) be the leaves obtained from a box \(B^0\) after finitely many operations replacing a box \(B\) by \(B\cap\{x:x_j\le s\}\) and \(B\cap\{x:x_j\ge s\}\), where \(s\) is interior to its selected interval. Every leaf is a closed axis-aligned box, \(B^0=\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal L}B\), and distinct leaf interiors are disjoint. Since intersections occur only on lower-dimensional split faces, \(\operatorname{vol}(B^0)=\sum_{B\in\mathcal L}\operatorname{vol}(B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive coordinate splits produce leaf boxes covering the root box with disjoint interiors and additive volume.

children.title: Coordinate-Selection Regimes

assumptions_latex: The current box is \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\) with at least one positive width.
A deterministic tie-breaking rule is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Longest-edge midpoint branching selects \(j\in\arg\max_i(u_i-\ell_i)\) and splits at \(s=(\ell_j+u_j)/2\); along every infinite branch, all widths converge to zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Longest-edge coordinate selection with midpoint splitting.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Cuts, Lower Bounds and Box Reduction p. 83

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\), compute \(w_i=u_i-\ell_i\), select \(j\in\arg\max_i w_i\) using the fixed tie rule, and set \(s=(\ell_j+u_j)/2\). Replace \(B\) by the two coordinate-split children and repeat on every unpruned descendant. Each selection halves a currently maximal width. Consequently, on any infinite nested sequence generated by this regime, every coordinate width and hence the box diameter converge to zero. The algorithm outputs the usual surviving nodes or incumbent when its external stopping test is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a longest side, bisect it, and repeat; every coordinate width vanishes along an infinite branch.

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 7. Cuts, Lower Bounds and Box Reduction p. 83

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General sufficient regime for vanishing widths along an infinite nested branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an infinite nested sequence of boxes generated by coordinate splits. Suppose every coordinate with positive initial width is selected infinitely often and some \(\alpha\in(0,1/2]\) satisfies \(\ell_i+\alpha(u_i-\ell_i)\le s\le u_i-\alpha(u_i-\ell_i)\) at every split of \([\ell_i,u_i]\). The selected child's width is at most \((1-\alpha)(u_i-\ell_i)\). Hence every coordinate width and the box diameter converge to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every coordinate is selected infinitely often and split points stay uniformly away from interval endpoints, all widths and the box diameter vanish.
assumptions_latex: The boxes form an infinite nested sequence generated by coordinate splits.
Every initially nonfixed coordinate is selected infinitely often.
There exists \(\alpha\in(0,1/2]\) such that every split is \(\alpha\)-balanced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall i,\ w_i^t\to0,\qquad \operatorname{diam}(B^t)\to0.

notation.meaning: Uniform balance parameter for split points.
Width of coordinate i at depth t.

children.title: Box-Shape Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Ineffective spatial refinement caused by poorly shaped rectangular regions.

assumptions_latex: The root box is \(B^0=[0,1]^2\).
Every descendant split bisects only coordinate \(x_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every descendant retains width one in coordinate \(x_2\), so its diameter is at least one and the partition mesh does not converge to zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent unsplit directions prevent vanishing box diameter.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Cuts, Lower Bounds and Box Reduction p. 83
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from \(B^0=[0,1]^2\) and, at every node, bisect only the \(x_1\)-interval. After \(t\) splits along any branch, the resulting box has side lengths \(2^{-t}\) and \(1\). Therefore \(\operatorname{diam}(B^t)=\sqrt{1+4^{-t}}\ge1\), although its volume tends to zero. Thus decreasing volume alone does not imply vanishing box diameter, and convergence results requiring every spatial direction to be refined cannot be invoked under this coordinate-starvation regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly shrinking only one side can drive volume to zero while leaving box diameter and an unsplit direction unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Box-Shape Degeneracy

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 7. Cuts, Lower Bounds and Box Reduction p. 83
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Aspect Ratio Excludes Box-Shape Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient geometric condition under which vanishing volume forces vanishing diameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B^t=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i^t,u_i^t]\) be nondegenerate boxes with widths \(w_i^t=u_i^t-\ell_i^t\). Suppose \(\max_iw_i^t\le\rho\min_iw_i^t\) for some fixed \(\rho\ge1\). If \(M_t=\max_iw_i^t\), then \(\operatorname{vol}(B^t)\ge M_t^n/\rho^{n-1}\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{vol}(B^t)\to0\) implies \(M_t\to0\) and \(\operatorname{diam}(B^t)\le\sqrt n M_t\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For boxes with uniformly bounded aspect ratio, vanishing volume implies vanishing diameter; degeneracy requires loss of shape regularity.
assumptions_latex: Each \(B^t\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nondegenerate axis-aligned box.
There exists \(\rho\ge1\) such that \(\max_iw_i^t\le\rho\min_iw_i^t\) for all \(t\).
\(\operatorname{vol}(B^t)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{diam}(B^t)\to0.

notation.meaning: Width of coordinate i in box B^t.

children.title: Binary Branching

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic binary branching at one search-tree node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Binary branching selects two predicates \(D_0\) and \(D_1\) such that \(R\subseteq D_0\cup D_1\) and \(R\cap D_0\cap D_1=\varnothing\). It creates the child regions \(R_j=R\cap D_j\) for \(j\in\{0,1\}\), and hence \(R=R_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}R_1\). For an integer-constrained variable \(x_i\) with fractional relaxation value \(\bar x_i\), the standard split uses \(D_0=\{x:x_i\leq\lfloor\bar x_i\rfloor\}\) and \(D_1=\{x:x_i\geq\lceil\bar x_i\rceil\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary branching replaces a node by two disjoint children covering its relaxation, commonly by splitting a fractional integer variable below its floor and above its ceiling.
assumptions_latex: The current node relaxation has feasible region \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
The predicates \(D_0\) and \(D_1\) are mutually exclusive on \(R\) and jointly cover \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The child regions satisfy \(R=R_0\mathbin{\dot\cup}R_1\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation, and Bounds p. 25

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation, and Bounds p. 25

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct coverage set for a floor-ceiling binary split at a fractional relaxation value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a node relaxation, let \(F=R\cap\{x:x_i\in\mathbb Z\}\), and let \(\bar x_i\notin\mathbb Z\). With \(D_0=\{x:x_i\le\lfloor\bar x_i\rfloor\}\) and \(D_1=\{x:x_i\ge\lceil\bar x_i\rceil\}\), one has \(F\subseteq D_0\cup D_1\) and \(F\cap D_0\cap D_1=\varnothing\), but generally \(R\nsubseteq D_0\cup D_1\). Thus the split is exhaustive for integer-feasible descendants and excludes the fractional slab, rather than partitioning the entire continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A floor-ceiling split covers all integer-feasible descendants, but generally does not cover the entire continuous relaxation between the floor and ceiling.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the current relaxation.
\(x_i\) is integer constrained in the target problem.
\(\bar x_i\notin\mathbb Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\subseteq D_0\cup D_1\quad\text{while generally}\quad R\nsubseteq D_0\cup D_1.

notation.meaning: Integer-feasible subset of the node relaxation with respect to the selected coordinate.

children.title: Multiway Branching
children.top_down_role: Search-space partitions producing more than two child subproblems.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiway Branching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite disjunctive branching with at least three nonempty children.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Multiway branching selects predicates \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\), where \(k\geq3\), such that \(R\subseteq\bigcup_{j=1}^kD_j\), \(R\cap D_j\cap D_\ell=\varnothing\) for \(j\neq\ell\), and \(R\cap D_j\neq\varnothing\) for every \(j\in\{1,cldots,k\}\). It creates the child regions \(R_j=R\cap D_j\), so \(R=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{j=1}^kR_j\). For an integer-constrained variable \(x_i\) with finite current domain \(V\), a partition \(V=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{j=1}^kV_j\) induces predicates \(D_j=\{x:x_i\in V_j\}\), provided every resulting child region is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiway branching partitions a node into at least three nonempty, pairwise-disjoint children covering the parent region, for example through a partition of an integer variable's finite current domain.
assumptions_latex: The current node relaxation has feasible region \(R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
A finite disjunction with \(k\geq3\) predicates covers \(R\), is mutually exclusive on \(R\), and induces \(k\) nonempty child regions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting regions satisfy \(R=\mathbin{\dot\bigcup}_{j=1}^kR_j\), with \(R_j\neq\varnothing\) for every \(j\).

children.title: Branching-Arity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tree-width, tree-depth, and node-processing consequences of partition arity.

knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Arity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact combinatorial tradeoff for a complete balanced search tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a complete \(k\)-ary rooted tree of depth \(d\), where \(k\geq2\) and \(d\geq0\), the leaf count and total node count are \(L=k^d\) and \(N=1+k+\cdots+k^d=(k^{d+1}-1)/(k-1)\). Given a target \(M\geq1\), the smallest depth of a complete \(k\)-ary tree having at least \(M\) leaves is \(\lceil\log_k M\rceil\). Thus greater arity can reduce the required complete-tree depth while causing each expanded internal node to generate more children. These identities alone do not rank branching arities by runtime, because pruning, imbalance, and child-solving costs may depend on \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For complete balanced trees, larger arity can reduce the depth needed to reach a target leaf capacity but creates more children per expansion; runtime also depends on pruning, imbalance, and child-solving costs.
assumptions_latex: The search tree is a complete rooted \(k\)-ary tree with \(k\geq2\).
Every leaf has the same depth \(d\geq0\).
The target leaf capacity is an integer \(M\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tree has \(L=k^d\) leaves and \(N=(k^{d+1}-1)/(k-1)\) total nodes, and its minimum depth for at least \(M\) leaves is \(\lceil\log_k M\rceil\).

notation.meaning: Actual numbers of leaves and total nodes.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation, and Bounds p. 25

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation, and Bounds p. 25

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact arity-dependent node count for finite full trees without a balance assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a finite rooted full \(k\)-ary tree, so every internal node has exactly \(k\ge2\) children. If \(I\) and \(L\) are its numbers of internal nodes and leaves, then \(kI=I+L-1\). Hence \(L=(k-1)I+1\) and \(|V(T)|=I+L=(kL-1)/(k-1)\). For an admissible fixed leaf count, larger \(k\) requires fewer internal expansions, but this identity does not compare pruning or node-processing costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite full k-ary tree has L=(k−1)I+1 leaves, exactly relating arity, internal expansions, and total nodes.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb Z\) and \(k\ge2\).
\(T\) is finite and every internal node has exactly \(k\) children.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L=(k-1)I+1,\qquad |V(T)|=\frac{kL-1}{k-1}.
knowledge_statements.title: Full k-ary Leaf–Internal-Node Identity
