knowledge_statements.scope_note: End-to-end elapsed time for a parallel branching search represented by a fixed computation DAG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W=C_0+\sum_{v\in V}C(v)\) be total work and let \(L\) be the span, the maximum cost of a dependency chain. On \(p\) identical processors, \(T_p\ge\max\{W/p,L\}\). Under a greedy work-conserving scheduler, \(T_p\le W/p+L\). Thus tree size and per-node work control total work but do not alone determine parallel elapsed time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel elapsed time depends on both total work and the critical dependency path; tree size times per-node cost controls work but not wall-clock time by itself.
assumptions_latex: The computation is represented by a finite, fixed dependency DAG.
\(W\) is total work and \(L\) is span.
The upper bound uses a greedy work-conserving scheduler on \(p\ge1\) identical processors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{W/p,L\}\le T_p\le W/p+L\).
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Work–Span Runtime Bound

children.title: Search-State Memory Complexity
children.top_down_role: Storage requirements for active nodes and reusable state.

children.title: Active-Frontier Storage
children.top_down_role: Storage requirements for live nodes awaiting processing.

assumptions_latex: At search time \(t\), the active frontier is the set \(F_t\) of generated but unresolved nodes.
Stored representation of node \(v\) occupies \(m(v)\ge 0\) memory units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Active-frontier storage is \(M_F(t)=\sum_{v\in F_t}m(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Memory occupied by generated nodes awaiting resolution.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At time \(t\), let \(F_t\) contain exactly the generated nodes that remain eligible for selection or further processing. If the stored state of node \(v\) occupies \(m(v)\) memory units, define \[M_F(t):=\sum_{v\in F_t}m(v).\] Shared global data and reusable workspaces are excluded from \(M_F(t)\) and accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Active-frontier storage is the total memory used by generated nodes that remain available for further search.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Frontier Storage

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage bound obtained from the number and encoded sizes of simultaneously active node records.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every time \(t\), if \(m(v)\le m_{\max}(t)\) for all \(v\in F_t\), then \[M_F(t)=\sum_{v\in F_t}m(v)\le |F_t|m_{\max}(t).\] If every active-node record has common size \(m\), then \(M_F(t)=m|F_t|\). Thus frontier cardinality controls storage only together with a node-record-size bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Frontier memory is at most the active-node count times the largest active-node record; node count alone does not control memory if record sizes can grow.
assumptions_latex: \(F_t\) is the active frontier at time \(t\).
Each active record has finite stored size \(m(v)\).
\(m_{\max}(t)=\max_{v\in F_t}m(v)\), with value zero when \(F_t=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_F(t)\le |F_t|m_{\max}(t)\).

notation.meaning: largest stored size of an active node at time t

knowledge_statements.title: Frontier-Cardinality Storage Bound

children.title: Reusable State Storage
children.top_down_role: Storage requirements for retained solver and node state.

assumptions_latex: At time \(t\), the algorithm retains a collection \(R_t\) of shared or recyclable search objects.
Object \(r\) occupies \(m(r)\ge 0\) memory units after shared ownership is counted once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reusable state storage is \(M_R(t)=\sum_{r\in R_t}m(r)\).

notation.meaning: retained reusable objects at time t
memory occupied by retained object r

review_flags: object ownership convention must prevent double counting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Storage for shared state retained across node-processing operations.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Continuous-Relaxation-Based Branch-and-Bound Methods p. 150

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At time \(t\), let \(R_t\) be the collection of retained objects reusable across nodes, such as global cuts, pseudocosts, cached factorizations, incumbent data, or solver workspaces. With shared objects counted once, define \[M_R(t):=\sum_{r\in R_t}m(r).\] State stored exclusively inside an active node belongs to frontier storage rather than \(M_R(t)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reusable state storage counts shared search data retained for use across multiple node-processing operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Reusable State Storage

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Continuous-Relaxation-Based Branch-and-Bound Methods p. 150

children.title: Peak Search Memory
children.top_down_role: Combined peak storage across frontier records and reusable state.

assumptions_latex: At every time \(t\), live memory decomposes into frontier storage \(M_F(t)\), reusable storage \(M_R(t)\), and other live storage \(M_O(t)\).
The three categories use a nonoverlapping ownership convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Peak search memory is \(M_{\mathrm{peak}}=\max_t\{M_F(t)+M_R(t)+M_O(t)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum simultaneously live memory during one search run.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under a nonoverlapping memory-accounting convention, let \(M_F(t)\), \(M_R(t)\), and \(M_O(t)\) denote active-frontier, reusable-state, and other live storage at time \(t\). Define \[M_{\mathrm{peak}}:=\max_t\bigl(M_F(t)+M_R(t)+M_O(t)\bigr).\] Because the maxima of the components need not occur simultaneously, summing their separate maxima gives only an upper bound on \(M_{\mathrm{peak}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Peak search memory is the largest simultaneous total of frontier, reusable, and other live storage during the run.
knowledge_statements.title: Peak Search Memory

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

children.title: Exponential Tree-Search Lower-Bound Family
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound families forcing large branch-and-bound trees.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Lower Bounds on the Size of General Branch-and-Bound Trees
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Lower Bounds on the Size of General Branch-and-Bound Trees

children.title: Variable-Branching Tree Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds for coordinate-branching trees.

assumptions_latex: Each internal node branches on one integer coordinate using \(x_j\le k\) and \(x_j\ge k+1\).
A witness set \(H\) of size \(M\) must be covered by terminal regions, and each terminal region contains at most one witness.
The completed search tree is binary and every internal node has two nonempty children.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every such tree has at least \(M\) leaves and at least \(2M-1\) generated nodes.
review_flags: source needed for a concrete exponential coordinate-branching family
current statement is a conditional witness-set lower-bound criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional leaf-count lower bound for binary coordinate branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a completed binary coordinate-branching tree whose internal split is \(x_j\le k\) versus \(x_j\ge k+1\). Let \(H\) be a set of \(M\) witness points covered by the terminal regions. If no terminal region can contain two distinct members of \(H\), then the number \(L\) of leaves satisfies \(L\ge M\). Since every internal node has two children, the generated size satisfies \[S=2L-1\ge 2M-1.\] Thus \(M=2^{\Omega(n)}\) yields an exponential tree-size lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If coordinate branching can place at most one of M required witnesses in each leaf, every completed binary tree has at least 2M−1 nodes.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Branching Tree Lower Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional witness-counting bound is mathematically coherent, but no source or concrete coordinate-branching family supports the exponential lower-bound claim associated with this leaf.

children.title: General-Disjunction Tree Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds persisting under general integral disjunctions.

assumptions_latex: Every internal node uses an integral disjunction with between \(2\) and \(q\) nonempty children, where \(q\ge 2\).
A witness set \(H\) of size \(M\) is covered by terminal regions, each containing at most one witness.
All generated internal nodes belong to the completed tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tree has at least \(M\) leaves and at least \(M+\lceil(M-1)/(q-1)\rceil\) generated nodes.
review_flags: source needed for a concrete family hard under general integral disjunctions
bounded disjunction arity is essential to the displayed node bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional lower bound for bounded-arity integral-disjunction trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every internal node apply an integral disjunction producing at most \(q\ge 2\) nonempty child regions. Suppose \(H\) contains \(M\) witnesses covered by the leaves and no leaf region contains two witnesses. Then the leaf count satisfies \(L\ge M\). For \(I\) internal nodes, the edge count gives \(I+L-1\le qI\), hence \(I\ge\lceil(L-1)/(q-1)\rceil\). Therefore \[S=I+L\ge M+\left\lceil\frac{M-1}{q-1}\right\rceil.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-arity disjunction tree separating M witnesses needs at least M leaves and a corresponding minimum number of internal nodes.
knowledge_statements.title: General-Disjunction Tree Lower Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-arity counting inequality is correct, but no evidence establishes a concrete family that remains hard under the stated class of integral disjunctions. Bounded arity is also essential to the displayed node bound.

children.title: Combinatorial Lower-Bound Family
children.top_down_role: Hard branch-and-bound instances from canonical combinatorial classes.

children.title: Packing Lower-Bound Families
children.top_down_role: Hard search-tree instances arising from packing structures.

assumptions_latex: For each size parameter \(n\), a packing instance admits a witness set \(H_n\).
Every valid terminal certificate covers at most one member of \(H_n\).
A complete branching certificate covers every member of \(H_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every complete tree has at least \(|H_n|\) leaves; if \(|H_n|\ge 2^{cn}\) for some \(c>0\), its tree size is exponential in \(n\).

notation.meaning: packing witnesses for instances of size n

review_flags: source needed for a concrete packing construction and its certificate-separation lemma
current statement records the abstract counting criterion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Witness-packing criterion for exponential branching-tree lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of packing instances indexed by \(n\), let \(H_n\) be a set of witnesses such that every valid terminal region or terminal certificate accounts for at most one member of \(H_n\), while completeness requires all witnesses to be accounted for. Then distinct witnesses require distinct leaves, so \[L_n\ge |H_n|.\] In particular, if \(|H_n|\ge 2^{cn}\) for some constant \(c>0\), every complete branching certificate has at least \(2^{cn}\) leaves and therefore exponential generated size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A packing family is exponentially hard when it has exponentially many witnesses and every valid terminal certificate can account for only one.
knowledge_statements.title: Packing Lower-Bound Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstract leaf-counting criterion is valid, but the exact leaf requires a sourced packing construction with exponentially many witnesses and a certificate-separation result. Neither is supplied.

children.title: Covering Lower-Bound Families
children.top_down_role: Hard search-tree instances arising from covering structures.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic tree-search proof system \(\mathcal P\) and a node-count size measure \(S_{\mathcal P}\) are fixed.
Each instance \(I_n\) is a binary covering formulation \(\min\{c_n^\top x:A_nx\ge b_n,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{d_n}\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family is a covering lower-bound family for \(\mathcal P\) precisely when \(S_{\mathcal P}(I_n)\ge 2^{\alpha n}\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).

notation.meaning: Minimum number of processed nodes required on an instance

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formal specialization of exponential tree-search lower bounds to binary covering instances
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines covering families by exponential node complexity in a fixed tree-search model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence \((I_n)_{n\ge1}\) is a covering lower-bound family for \(\mathcal P\) if every \(I_n\) has the form \(\min\{c_n^\top x:A_nx\ge b_n,\ x\in\{0,1\}^{d_n}\}\), with \(A_n\ge0\) and \(b_n\ge0\), and there exist constants \(\alpha>0\) and \(n_0\) such that \(S_{\mathcal P}(I_n)\ge 2^{\alpha n}\) for every \(n\ge n_0\). The parameter \(n\) must be polynomially related to the encoded input length, so the inequality expresses exponential rather than padding-induced growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covering lower-bound family consists of nonnegative binary covering instances for which every search proof in the fixed model uses exponentially many nodes.
knowledge_statements.title: Covering Lower-Bound Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the covering lower-bound leaf, but no source supports this particular formulation. The asserted relationship between n and encoded input length is also too ambiguous to establish exponential complexity in the intended size measure.

children.title: Routing Lower-Bound Families
children.top_down_role: Hard search-tree instances arising from routing structures.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic tree-search proof system \(\mathcal P\) and node-count measure \(S_{\mathcal P}\) are fixed.
Each \(I_n\) is a mixed-integer formulation of a routing problem on a graph \(G_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family is routing-hard for \(\mathcal P\) when \(S_{\mathcal P}(I_n)\ge2^{\alpha n}\) eventually, with \(n\) polynomially related to input length.

notation.meaning: Minimum search-tree size for an instance

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formal specialization of exponential tree-search lower bounds to routing formulations
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses formulation-specific tree size; different routing formulations need not have comparable bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence \((I_n)_{n\ge1}\) is a routing lower-bound family for \(\mathcal P\) if each \(I_n\) encodes feasible routes in a graph \(G_n\), the encoding length is polynomial in \(n\), and there are constants \(\alpha>0\) and \(n_0\) such that \(S_{\mathcal P}(I_n)\ge2^{\alpha n}\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). The formulation, relaxation, admissible branching disjunctions, node-selection rule, and pruning certificates are part of \(\mathcal P\); changing any of them defines a different lower-bound assertion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A routing lower-bound family has polynomial-size routing formulations whose minimum search trees in a specified proof system are exponentially large.
knowledge_statements.title: Routing Lower-Bound Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The role and definition kind fit the leaf, but the routing problem and formulation class are not fixed precisely enough, and no source supports the proposed lower-bound convention. The treatment of node selection inside a minimum-tree measure also requires clarification.

children.title: Perturbation-Stable Hardness Family
children.top_down_role: Tree-size hardness persisting under coefficient perturbations.

children.title: Perturbation-Robust Hardness
children.top_down_role: Tree-size hardness persisting across bounded coefficient perturbations.

assumptions_latex: Instances are represented by data vectors \(z_n\in\mathbb R^{m_n}\), with perturbations measured by a norm \(\|\cdot\|\).
A search model \(\mathcal P\) and size measure \(S_{\mathcal P}\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Robust hardness holds when an entire neighborhood \(B(z_n,\rho_n)\) retains the lower bound \(S_{\mathcal P}\ge2^{\alpha n}\).

notation.meaning: Search resource required by the fixed model

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: neighborhood-uniform definition of perturbation robustness
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A worst-case, neighborhood-uniform notion; it does not average over perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The family \((z_n)_{n\ge1}\) has perturbation-robust exponential hardness for \(\mathcal P\) at radii \((\rho_n)_{n\ge1}\) if there exist \(\alpha>0\) and \(n_0\) such that, for every \(n\ge n_0\) and every valid data vector \(z\) satisfying \(\|z-z_n\|\le\rho_n\), one has \(S_{\mathcal P}(z)\ge2^{\alpha n}\). Validity includes preservation of the declared variable domains and encoding conventions. A meaningful robustness claim must state the norm, perturbed coefficients, radius scale, and treatment of invalid perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardness is perturbation-robust when every valid instance in a specified neighborhood still requires an exponentially large search tree.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation-Robust Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The neighborhood-uniform condition matches perturbation-robust hardness, but its mathematical force depends on the coefficient representation, norm, admissible perturbations, and radius scale. No specialized source establishes the proposed definition.

children.title: Smoothed Search Hardness
children.top_down_role: Search hardness assessed under randomized perturbation regimes.

assumptions_latex: For each base instance \(z\), a perturbation distribution \(D_{z,\sigma}\) with scale \(\sigma>0\) is specified.
A search model \(\mathcal P\), size measure \(S_{\mathcal P}\), and dimension parameter \(n\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Smoothed exponential hardness means \(\sup_z\mathbb E[S_{\mathcal P}(Z)]\ge2^{\alpha n}\) for the declared perturbation regime.

notation.meaning: Search resource in the fixed model

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: expected resource lower bound in the smoothed-analysis quantifier order
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines expected smoothed hardness; tail-probability lower bounds are distinct claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a declared scale regime \(\Sigma_n\), the smoothed search complexity is \(\mathcal S_{\mathcal P}(n,\sigma)=\sup_{z\in\mathcal I_n}\mathbb E_{Z\sim D_{z,\sigma}}[S_{\mathcal P}(Z)]\). The model exhibits smoothed exponential hardness if there are \(\alpha>0\), \(n_0\), and scales \(\sigma_n\in\Sigma_n\) such that \(\mathcal S_{\mathcal P}(n,\sigma_n)\ge2^{\alpha n}\) for all \(n\ge n_0\). The assertion must fix coefficient normalization, perturbation distribution, conditioning or truncation used to preserve valid instances, and whether arithmetic or bit complexity is counted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smoothed search hardness occurs when the worst base instance still has exponential expected search cost after perturbation at specified scales.
knowledge_statements.title: Smoothed Search Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A complexity-bound record fits the leaf, but the existential choice of one scale sequence can materially weaken smoothed hardness. A source is needed to confirm the quantifier order, perturbation regime, validity conditioning, and complexity measure.

children.title: Hardness Fragility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Perturbation regimes under which large-tree constructions cease to persist.

assumptions_latex: A hard base family \((z_n)\), perturbation model \(D_{z_n,\sigma}\), and search model \(\mathcal P\) are fixed.
Unperturbed instances satisfy \(S_{\mathcal P}(z_n)\ge2^{\alpha n}\) for some \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fragility is witnessed when vanishing perturbations reduce a superpolynomial lower bound to polynomial expected search size.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: asymptotic boundary separating worst-case hardness from perturbation-stable hardness
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Captures collapse under asymptotically small random perturbations, not merely a changed constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exponential hardness of \((z_n)\) is fragile under \((D_{z_n,\sigma})\) if there exist scales \(\sigma_n>0\) with \(\sigma_n\to0\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(\mathbb E_{Z\sim D_{z_n,\sigma_n}}[S_{\mathcal P}(Z)]\le p(n)\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), despite \(S_{\mathcal P}(z_n)\ge2^{\alpha n}\). A fragility boundary is a scale function \(\sigma_*(n)\) separating a regime with a proved superpolynomial lower bound from one with a proved polynomial upper bound; an unresolved interval is permitted and must be stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hardness is fragile when perturbations tending to zero turn exponential unperturbed search into polynomial expected search; a boundary separates proved regimes.
knowledge_statements.title: Hardness Fragility Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container, but the proposed collapse criterion and boundary definition are specialized and unsupported. Their validity depends on the perturbation distribution, normalization, and scale quantifiers.

children.title: Tree-Search Proof-System Interpretation
children.top_down_role: Interpretation of search trees as structured optimization and infeasibility proofs.

children.title: Tree-Like Infeasibility Refutations
children.top_down_role: Search trees interpreted as hierarchical infeasibility proofs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Soundness of a Closed Tree-Like Refutation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness of finite exhaustive disjunction trees with certified infeasible leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite rooted tree start from a mixed-integer system F. At every internal node, suppose the child restrictions cover every mixed-integer point satisfying the accumulated node system. If every leaf's accumulated system is certified infeasible, then F is infeasible. Conversely, a finite tree with an uncovered feasible case or an uncertified leaf does not, from the tree data alone, certify root infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exhaustive branching and certified infeasibility at every leaf imply root infeasibility; missing coverage or an uncertified leaf breaks the certificate.
assumptions_latex: The tree is finite.
Every internal branching disjunction covers all mixed-integer points satisfying its accumulated node system.
Every leaf has a sound infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\text{complete branch coverage}\bigr)\land\bigl(\text{all leaves infeasible}\bigr)\Rightarrow F=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Soundness of a Closed Tree-Like Refutation

assumptions_latex: The integer-feasibility set is \(F=\{x\in\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q:Ax\le b\}\).
Every internal node applies an admissible disjunction whose branches cover all integer points satisfying the node constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A closed tree with infeasible leaves is a tree-like refutation of \(F\ne\varnothing\), and its size is its number of nodes.

notation.meaning: Constraint system accumulated at node v
Branching disjunction at an internal node

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a finite branch-and-bound infeasibility tree as a tree-like proof.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree-like infeasibility refutation of \(F\) is a finite rooted tree. The root carries \(C_r=\{Ax\le b\}\). If node \(v\) carries \(C_v\), its children carry \(C_v\cup D_{v,j}\), where the admissible disjunction \(\bigvee_{j=1}^{k_v}D_{v,j}\) is valid for every mixed-integer point satisfying \(C_v\). Every leaf must possess a verifiable certificate that its accumulated system contains no point of \(\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q\). Because derived subtrees are not shared, the refutation is tree-like. Its node count equals the associated exhaustive branching-search size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching tree refutes feasibility when its disjunctions cover all integer possibilities and every leaf has a verifiable infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Tree-Like Infeasibility Refutations

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the topic, but the cited general branch-and-bound outline does not clearly support the exact tree-like proof-system definition, admissible-disjunction semantics, or equality between refutation node count and exhaustive search size. A proof-complexity or branch-and-bound proof-system source is required.

children.title: Branching-Strength Hierarchies
children.top_down_role: Comparisons among proof systems induced by different branching classes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Simulation and Separation of Branching Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic comparison under fixed instance encoding, proof-size measure, and leaf-certificate convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S_i(I) be the minimum size of a \mathcal B_i-refutation of an infeasible encoded instance I. The system \mathcal B_2 polynomially simulates \mathcal B_1 if there is a polynomial p such that S_2(I)\le p(|I|,S_1(I)) for every applicable I. The systems are polynomially equivalent when each simulates the other. A family (I_n) separates \mathcal B_1 from \mathcal B_2 when S_2(I_n) is polynomially bounded in |I_n| but S_1(I_n) is superpolynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial simulation compares minimum refutation sizes under common conventions; a separation family has polynomial proofs in one branching system and superpolynomial proofs in the other.
assumptions_latex: The systems use the same instance encoding, proof-size convention, and sound leaf-certificate semantics.
Only infeasible instances admitting the referenced refutations are compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal B_2\text{ simulates }\mathcal B_1\iff \exists p\text{ polynomial}:S_2(I)\le p(|I|,S_1(I))\text{ for all applicable }I.

notation.meaning: Minimum refutation size under branching class i

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Simulation and Separation of Branching Systems

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Branching-Class Inclusion Need Not Be Strict
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on conclusions obtainable solely from inclusion of admissible branching rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \mathcal B_1\subseteq\mathcal B_2 under identical proof conventions, then inclusion yields only S_{\mathcal B_2}(I)\le S_{\mathcal B_1}(I). It does not imply strict inequality on any instance or an asymptotic separation; equality can hold when every additional rule has a size-preserving simulation in \mathcal B_1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Additional branching rules cannot worsen minimum proof size, but they need not yield any strict improvement.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal B_1\subseteq\mathcal B_2.
Both systems use identical proof-size and leaf-certificate conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal B_1\subseteq\mathcal B_2\not\Rightarrow\exists I:\ S_{\mathcal B_2}(I)<S_{\mathcal B_1}(I).

notation.meaning: Minimum refutation size under branching class \mathcal B

knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Class Inclusion Need Not Be Strict

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global size simulation without duplicating descendant subproofs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every \(\mathcal B_1\)-branch occurring at a reachable region has a \(\mathcal B_2\)-simulation subtree of at most \(g(|I|)\) nodes whose leaves correspond one-to-one to the original branch children, induce the same child regions, and preserve the leaf-certificate convention. Replacing every internal node of a size-\(s\) \(\mathcal B_1\)-refutation by its simulation and attaching each original child subtree to its unique corresponding leaf yields a \(\mathcal B_2\)-refutation of size at most \(g(|I|)s\). Without the one-to-one attachment condition, descendant subproofs may require duplication and this bound need not follow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded local simulations give a multiplicative global size bound only when each original child subtree attaches uniquely and proof semantics are preserved.
assumptions_latex: Every simulated branch has at most \(g(|I|)\) nodes.
Simulation leaves correspond one-to-one to the original children and induce the same restricted regions.
Leaf-certificate and size conventions are preserved.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{\mathcal B_2}(I)\le g(|I|)S_{\mathcal B_1}(I)

notation.meaning: uniform size bound for an interface-preserving local simulation

review_flags: The multiplicative conclusion is not valid for arbitrary local cover simulations that duplicate original child subproofs.
knowledge_statements.title: Interface-Preserving Local Simulation Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum refutation-size comparison under identical proof conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathcal B_1\subseteq\mathcal B_2\), and both systems use the same instance encoding, size measure, branch semantics, and leaf certificates, then every \(\mathcal B_1\)-refutation is a \(\mathcal B_2\)-refutation of the same size. Hence \[S_{\mathcal B_2}(I)\le S_{\mathcal B_1}(I)\] for every infeasible instance \(I\) admitting such a refutation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing every branch available to a weaker system cannot increase minimum refutation size when all proof conventions agree.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal B_1\subseteq\mathcal B_2
Both systems use identical instance, size, branching, and leaf-certificate conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{\mathcal B_2}(I)\le S_{\mathcal B_1}(I)

notation.meaning: minimum refutation size for instance I using branching class B

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Under Branching-Class Inclusion

assumptions_latex: Two branching classes \(\mathcal B_1\subseteq\mathcal B_2\) use the same leaf certificates and size convention.
For an infeasible system \(I\), \(S_{\mathcal B}(I)\) denotes minimum refutation-tree size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Branching-class inclusion implies \(S_{\mathcal B_2}(I)\le S_{\mathcal B_1}(I)\) for every infeasible \(I\).

notation.meaning: Minimum refutation size using a branching class

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simulation by inclusion of admissible branching rules
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States monotonicity only; strict hierarchy separations require explicit lower-bound families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\mathcal B_1\subseteq\mathcal B_2\), every tree-like refutation using \(\mathcal B_1\) is also a valid refutation using \(\mathcal B_2\), without changing its nodes or leaf certificates. Consequently, for every infeasible instance \(I\), \(S_{\mathcal B_2}(I)\le S_{\mathcal B_1}(I)\). More generally, if each \(\mathcal B_1\)-branching node can be simulated by a \(\mathcal B_2\)-subtree of at most \(g(n)\) nodes on inputs of size \(n\), then a size-\(s\) \(\mathcal B_1\)-refutation yields a \(\mathcal B_2\)-refutation of size at most \(g(n)s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing more branching disjunctions cannot increase minimum refutation size; bounded local simulations yield corresponding global size simulations.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Strength Hierarchies

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Branching-class monotonicity is mathematically plausible and fits the hierarchy topic, but there is no citation. The stronger g(n)s simulation assertion additionally needs precise preservation of branch outcomes, leaf certificates, and the input-size parameter.

children.title: Search Performance Stability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Implementation and instance effects not captured by coarse worst-case measures.

children.title: Model-Data Sensitivity Family
children.top_down_role: Tree-size variation caused by modeling choices and small data changes.

children.title: Instance Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Tree-size variation across problem instances and small data changes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Worst-Case Complexity Does Not Determine Individual-Instance Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates class-wide worst-case resource bounds from variation among particular instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed algorithm \(\mathcal A\), let \(R_{\mathcal A}(I)\) be its resource use on \(I\in\mathcal I_n\) and \(W_{\mathcal A}(n)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I_n}R_{\mathcal A}(I)\). Knowledge of \(W_{\mathcal A}(n)\) alone determines neither \(R_{\mathcal A}(I)\) for a specified instance nor the resource ratio between two instances in \(\mathcal I_n\). Thus a worst-case bound is not an instance-sensitivity bound without a declared comparison relation or distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A worst-case bound for an instance class does not quantify resource variation between particular instances.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm, resource convention, size parameter, and instance class are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathcal A}(n)\text{ alone does not determine pairwise instance sensitivity}.

notation.meaning: Resource used by algorithm A on instance I.
Worst resource use over the size-n instance class.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Complexity Does Not Determine Individual-Instance Cost

assumptions_latex: A deterministic solver configuration \(\mathcal A\) and resource measure \(R_{\mathcal A}\) are fixed.
Instances of size parameter \(n\) belong to a declared class \(\mathcal I_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Instance sensitivity is the variation of \(R_{\mathcal A}\) over instances in \(\mathcal I_n\) under a declared comparison relation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: resource variation under fixed algorithm and varying instances
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Holds the formulation and complete solver configuration fixed while the instance varies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a comparison relation \(\sim_n\) on \(\mathcal I_n\), the multiplicative instance sensitivity of \(\mathcal A\) is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{inst}}(n)=\sup\{R_{\mathcal A}(I)/\max\{1,R_{\mathcal A}(J)\}:I,J\in\mathcal I_n,\ I\sim_n J\}\). The relation may require equal dimensions, equal combinatorial type, or a bounded data distance, but it must be declared. A family is polynomially instance-stable when \(\kappa_{\mathrm{inst}}(n)\le p(n)\) for some polynomial \(p\); it is superpolynomially sensitive when no such bound holds along an infinite subsequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Instance sensitivity measures how much a fixed solver's search resource varies between instances regarded as comparable at the same size.
knowledge_statements.title: Instance Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the multiplicative modulus and the infinite-subsequence criterion are proposed conventions rather than established sourced terminology. The result also depends essentially on a concrete comparison relation.

children.title: Formulation Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Search variation caused by alternative formulations of the same problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relaxation Strength Does Not Alone Order Search Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates relaxation dominance from end-to-end branch-and-bound performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) and \(G\) be exact formulations of the same minimization problem, with valid root bounds \(L_F\le L_G\). Root-bound dominance alone is insufficient to conclude \(R(G)\le R(F)\) for node count, relaxation solves, memory, or runtime, because auxiliary variables, admissible branching, per-node work, presolve, cut generation, and incumbent discovery need not be controlled by that dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger root relaxation alone does not guarantee a smaller or faster branch-and-bound search.
assumptions_latex: The formulations encode the same optimization problem under a stated projection and objective correspondence.
Both root bounds are valid for minimization.
No additional correspondence between their search mechanisms is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_G\ge L_F\;\not\Rightarrow\;R(G)\le R(F).

notation.meaning: Valid root lower bounds for formulations F and G.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Strength Does Not Alone Order Search Cost

assumptions_latex: Two formulations \(F\) and \(G\) encode the same feasible solutions after projection.
The search configuration and node-count convention are transferred identically except for formulation-dependent relaxations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Formulation sensitivity is measured by the ratio between \(S(F)\) and \(S(G)\) for equivalent formulations.

notation.meaning: Search resource under the fixed configuration

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: comparison of search size across projection-equivalent formulations
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concerns equivalent models, including extended formulations, under a controlled solver configuration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and \(G\subseteq\mathbb R^{d+r}\) be mixed-integer formulations with \(\operatorname{proj}_x(G)=F\), including agreement of objective values under projection. Their symmetric formulation-sensitivity factor is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{form}}(F,G)=\max\{S(F)/\max\{1,S(G)\},S(G)/\max\{1,S(F)\}\}\). A formulation family is polynomially stable if this factor is polynomially bounded for every declared pair; an unbounded or exponential factor witnesses sensitivity. Comparisons must include encoding length and specify how branching on auxiliary variables is treated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Formulation sensitivity compares search size for projection-equivalent models while controlling encoding, solver settings, and branching on auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Formulation Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record belongs in the formulation-sensitivity leaf, but no source supports this symmetric ratio as the defining measure. Projection and objective agreement alone do not fully specify correspondence of integer domains, encodings, branching permissions, and solver behavior.

children.title: Data-Perturbation Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Performance changes under controlled modifications of input data.

assumptions_latex: Instances are represented by data vectors \(z\in\mathcal Z\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) with metric \(d\).
A deterministic search configuration \(\mathcal A\) and positive resource measure \(R_{\mathcal A}\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local sensitivity modulus \(\omega(z,\varepsilon)\) quantifies the largest resource ratio caused by perturbations of radius \(\varepsilon\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local modulus for algorithmic resource sensitivity under data perturbations
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures local worst-case variation and differs from expected smoothed complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\omega(z,\varepsilon)=\sup\{\max\{R_{\mathcal A}(z')/R_{\mathcal A}(z),R_{\mathcal A}(z)/R_{\mathcal A}(z')\}:z'\in\mathcal Z,\ d(z,z')\le\varepsilon\}\). The search procedure is locally polynomially stable at \(z\) over radii \(\varepsilon_n\) when \(\omega(z,\varepsilon_n)\le p(n)\) for a polynomial \(p\). It is data-perturbation sensitive when arbitrarily small admissible perturbations produce superpolynomial resource ratios. The data coordinates, normalization, metric, and rules for preserving integrality and feasibility conventions must be specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Data-perturbation sensitivity is the largest search-cost ratio between an instance and valid nearby data under a declared metric.
knowledge_statements.title: Data-Perturbation Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local resource-ratio concept fits data-perturbation sensitivity, but it is unsupported by a source. The stability clause invokes n although the record does not connect z or the radii to an instance-size sequence indexed by n.

children.title: Search-Policy Sensitivity Family
children.top_down_role: Performance variation caused by search-policy choices.

children.title: Branching-Policy Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Performance variation caused by branching-policy choices.

assumptions_latex: A formulation \(I\), traversal rule \(\tau\), pruning rules, and all nonbranching solver choices are fixed.
Policies \(\beta\) belong to a declared admissible branching-policy class \(\mathfrak B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Branching-policy sensitivity is the worst ratio of \(R(I;\beta,\tau)\) over policies \(\beta\in\mathfrak B\).

notation.meaning: Search resource for the selected policies

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: controlled policy comparison using a resource ratio
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Varies branching choices only; traversal and all remaining solver mechanisms stay fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The branching-policy sensitivity on \(I\) is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{br}}(I)=\sup_{\beta_1,\beta_2\in\mathfrak B}R(I;\beta_1,\tau)/\max\{1,R(I;\beta_2,\tau)\}\). Here each \(\beta\) maps the current search state to an admissible branching disjunction, including deterministic tie-breaking. A class \((\mathcal I_n)\) is polynomially branching-stable if \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I_n}\kappa_{\mathrm{br}}(I)\le p(n)\) for some polynomial \(p\); it is exponentially sensitive if this supremum is at least \(2^{\alpha n}\) along an infinite subsequence for some \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branching-policy sensitivity compares search resources across admissible branching rules while traversal, pruning, formulation, and tie-breaking conventions remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Policy Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and controlled comparison fit branching-policy sensitivity, but the proposed ratio and asymptotic classifications lack a source. The admissible policy class, state information, and tie-breaking conventions materially affect the claim.

children.title: Traversal-Policy Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Performance variation caused by node-selection choices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies a regime in which open-node order cannot change completed generated-node or processed-node counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a finite rooted search tree whose child generation and closure status are determined solely by each node's inherited state, independently of incumbents, processing history, and traversal order. If every generated open node is eventually processed, every exhaustive traversal processes the same node set. Thus generated-node and processed-node counts are traversal-invariant, although processing order and memory use may differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When node generation and closure are independent of incumbents and processing history, exhaustive traversal changes order but not the completed generated or processed node set.
assumptions_latex: The potential search tree is finite.
Child generation and node closure are traversal-independent.
Every generated open node is eventually processed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{gen}}(\tau_1)=N_{\mathrm{gen}}(\tau_2)\quad\text{and}\quad N_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau_1)=N_{\mathrm{proc}}(\tau_2).

notation.meaning: Number of nodes generated under traversal policy tau.
Number of nodes processed under traversal policy tau.

knowledge_statements.title: Traversal Invariance Under Order-Independent Closure

assumptions_latex: A formulation \(I\), branching policy \(\beta\), pruning rules, and all other solver choices are fixed.
Traversal policies \(\tau\) belong to a declared class \(\mathfrak T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Traversal sensitivity is the worst resource ratio \(R(I;\beta,\tau_1)/R(I;\beta,\tau_2)\) over \(\tau_1,\tau_2\in\mathfrak T\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: controlled traversal-policy comparison using a resource ratio
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Varies open-node selection only; incumbent effects make the resource convention essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The traversal-policy sensitivity on \(I\) is \(\kappa_{\mathrm{trav}}(I)=\sup_{\tau_1,\tau_2\in\mathfrak T}R(I;\beta,\tau_1)/\max\{1,R(I;\beta,\tau_2)\}\). Each \(\tau\) selects the next open node using only the declared search state and deterministic tie-breaking. The definition must specify whether \(R\) counts generated nodes, processed nodes, relaxation solves, or time, because traversal can change incumbent discovery and hence pruning. Polynomial stability and exponential sensitivity mean respectively polynomial and exponential bounds on \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I_n}\kappa_{\mathrm{trav}}(I)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Traversal-policy sensitivity compares search costs across open-node selection rules while branching and all other solver mechanisms remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Traversal-Policy Sensitivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits traversal-policy sensitivity, but the proposed modulus is unsourced. Generated nodes, processed nodes, relaxation solves, and time can behave differently under traversal because incumbent discovery affects pruning, so a fixed resource convention and supporting source are essential.

children.title: Policy-Interaction Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Performance variation arising from combinations of branching and traversal policies.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additive Policy Interaction Depends on Resource Scale
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits conclusions drawn from additive interaction measured using one search resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) and \(Q\) be resource measures evaluated on the same four branching-traversal policy pairs, and let \(\Delta_R\) and \(\Delta_Q\) be their additive cross-differences. Even when \(Q=\phi(R)\), the equality \(\Delta_R=0\) need not imply \(\Delta_Q=0\) if \(\phi\) is nonlinear. Consequently, absence, sign, and magnitude of additive policy interaction are meaningful only on the declared resource scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interaction measured with node count need not agree with interaction measured using runtime or a nonlinear transformation of node count.
assumptions_latex: All four policy pairs are evaluated on the same instance and under the same computational conventions.
Interaction is represented by an additive cross-difference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta_R=0\;\not\Rightarrow\;\Delta_Q=0\quad\text{for a general nonlinear transformation}.

notation.meaning: Additive interaction contrasts for resources R and Q.

knowledge_statements.title: Additive Policy Interaction Depends on Resource Scale
Policy-Interaction Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interaction between branching and traversal policies, measured with the instance and computational realization fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an instance \(I\), computational realization \(\omega\), branching policies \(b_0,b_1\), and traversal policies \(t_0,t_1\). For a search-resource measure \(R\), define the policy-interaction contrast by \[\Delta_R=R(I,b_1,t_1;\omega)-R(I,b_1,t_0;\omega)-R(I,b_0,t_1;\omega)+R(I,b_0,t_0;\omega).\] The resource is additively policy-separable on these choices only if \(\Delta_R=0\). A nonzero contrast therefore records sensitivity that cannot be attributed to an isolated branching-policy effect or an isolated traversal-policy effect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cross-difference of four matched runs measures whether branching and traversal policies jointly affect resource use beyond their separate additive effects.
assumptions_latex: \(R(I,b,t;\omega)\) is finite for all four policy pairs.
The instance, stopping rule, implementation, and realization \(\omega\) are held fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Delta_R\ne 0\) implies nonadditive policy-interaction sensitivity.

notation.meaning: Search resource, such as processed nodes or runtime.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this formal interaction-sensitivity measure.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cross-difference is mathematically coherent and fits the property container, but no cited source supports this formal sensitivity measure.

children.title: Computational Nondeterminism
children.top_down_role: Run-to-run variation arising from parallelism, tie-breaking, and numerical effects.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Execution Variation Does Not Imply Incorrectness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates run-to-run execution variation from validity of independently certified terminal claims.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If two admissible executions with identical declared inputs produce outputs or traces \(Y_1\ne Y_2\), computational variation is present, but mathematical error does not follow. When each terminal claim satisfies the same declared feasibility and optimality certificate, both executions may be valid even if their search trees, runtimes, or selected optimal solutions differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different runs can follow different searches or return different optimal solutions without being incorrect, provided every terminal claim satisfies the required certificate.
assumptions_latex: The declared instance, solver configuration, and stopping criterion are identical.
Each terminal claim is checked against the same feasibility and optimality standard.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Y_1\ne Y_2\;\not\Rightarrow\;\text{either execution is mathematically invalid}.

notation.meaning: Output or execution trace from run r.

knowledge_statements.title: Execution Variation Does Not Imply Incorrectness
Computational Nondeterminism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Run-to-run resource variation under fixed declared inputs and search settings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a fixed optimization instance and \(p\) a fixed declared solver policy. Let \(\Omega(I,p)\) contain computational realizations induced by admissible thread schedules, unresolved ties, and floating-point execution paths. For a reported search output or resource \(Y(I,p;\omega)\), computational nondeterminism is present when there exist \(\omega_1,\omega_2\in\Omega(I,p)\) such that \[Y(I,p;\omega_1)\ne Y(I,p;\omega_2).\] If \(Y\) is random under a specified realization law, its run-to-run variability may be summarized by its distribution or, when finite, by \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid I,p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computation is nondeterministic when identical declared inputs and policies can produce different outputs or resource measurements through admissible execution realizations.
assumptions_latex: The declared instance \(I\), solver policy \(p\), and stopping rule are fixed.
Only admissible implementation-level realizations vary between runs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Computational nondeterminism holds exactly when \(Y(I,p;\cdot)\) is nonconstant on \(\Omega(I,p)\).
review_flags: The supplied sources do not address parallel, numerical, or tie-breaking nondeterminism.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the terminal context, but its treatment of scheduling, tie-breaking, floating-point paths, and realization laws has no supplied source.

children.title: Pure-Integer LP-Based Search
children.top_down_role: LP-based branch-and-bound for pure integer models.

knowledge_statements.title: Pure-Integer LP-Based Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP-based branch-and-bound for bounded pure-integer linear minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\ge b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), initialize the active list with the root LP relaxation and the incumbent value \(U=+\infty\). Repeatedly select a node, solve its LP relaxation, and prune it if infeasible or if its lower bound is at least \(U\). If an optimal LP solution \(\bar x\) is integral, update the incumbent. Otherwise choose an index \(j\) with \(\bar x_j\notin\mathbb Z\) and create children imposing \(x_j\le\lfloor\bar x_j\rfloor\) and \(x_j\ge\lceil\bar x_j\rceil\). Stop when the active list is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve LP relaxations at tree nodes, prune by infeasibility or incumbent bounds, and branch on a fractional integer variable until no active nodes remain.
assumptions_latex: The integer-variable bounds \(\ell,u\) are finite and integral.
Every node LP is solved to a certified optimum or certified infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Upon exhaustion of the active list, the incumbent is globally optimal, or infeasibility is certified if no incumbent exists.

notation.meaning: Best incumbent objective value for minimization.
Optimal solution of the current node LP relaxation.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Continuous-Relaxation-Based Branch-and-Bound Methods p. 150

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Continuous-Relaxation-Based Branch-and-Bound Methods p. 150

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite assignment-tree bound for the bounded pure-integer algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \([\ell,u]\cap\mathbb Z^n\), let \(D=\prod_{j=1}^n(u_j-\ell_j+1)\). Under exhaustive floor–ceiling branching, the assignment-partition tree has at most \(D\) nonempty terminal integer-domain cells and at most \(2D-1\) nodes. This is an enumeration bound rather than a polynomial bound in binary input length, since \(D\) may be exponential in that length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded pure-integer LP search has at most one terminal assignment cell per lattice assignment, but the resulting bound can be exponential in the input encoding.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z^n\) are finite.
Branching uses exhaustive floor–ceiling splits on fractional integer coordinates.
Every processed node LP returns a certified status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{terminal}}\le D,\qquad N_{\mathrm{nodes}}\le2D-1.

notation.meaning: Number of lattice assignments in the bounded box.

children.title: Mixed-Integer LP-Based Search
children.top_down_role: LP-based branch-and-bound for mixed discrete-continuous models.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer LP-Based Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: LP-based branch-and-bound with both integer-constrained and continuous variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x+d^{\mathsf T}y:Ax+By\ge b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^p,\ y\in\mathbb R^q\}\), maintain active nodes defined by restrictions on \(x\) and an incumbent value \(U\). At a selected node, solve the LP relaxation obtained by replacing \(x\in\mathbb Z^p\) with \(x\in\mathbb R^p\). Prune an infeasible node or one whose LP lower bound is at least \(U\). If the relaxed optimizer has integral \(x\), update the incumbent; otherwise branch on a fractional component of \(x\). Continuous components of \(y\) are optimized but never require integrality branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed-integer branch-and-bound relaxes only integrality, branches on fractional discrete variables, and retains continuous variables in every node LP.
assumptions_latex: Each node LP has a certified optimum or certified infeasibility.
Branching restrictions eventually exclude the current fractional integer assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the active tree is exhausted, the final incumbent is globally optimal, or the model is infeasible when no incumbent exists.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Continuous-Relaxation-Based Branch-and-Bound Methods p. 150

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Mixed-Integer LP Search Under Bounded Discrete Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-search guarantee determined by the bounded integer coordinates despite the presence of continuous variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\ell_j\le x_j\le u_j\) with finite integral bounds and every branch uses the exhaustive split \(x_j\le\lfloor\bar x_j\rfloor\) or \(x_j\ge\lceil\bar x_j\rceil\). Let \(D=\prod_{j=1}^p(u_j-\ell_j+1)\). The resulting assignment-partition tree has at most \(D\) nonempty terminal integer-domain cells and at most \(2D-1\) nodes. Continuous variables do not change this combinatorial bound. Without finite integer domains or another well-founded termination argument, this bound does not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded integer domains make the mixed-integer LP assignment tree finite; continuous variables do not enlarge it, while unbounded discrete domains require another termination argument.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z^p\) are finite.
Branching uses exhaustive floor–ceiling splits on fractional integer coordinates.
Every processed node LP returns a certified status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{terminal}}\le D,\qquad N_{\mathrm{nodes}}\le2D-1.

children.title: Tree-Cut Coordination Interface
children.top_down_role: Boundary between tree search and dynamically strengthened polyhedral relaxations.

children.title: Node-Level Cut Separation
children.top_down_role: Generation of relaxation-strengthening cuts during node processing.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inference boundary when a node separator returns no violated cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal C_v\) be a normalized cut family valid for the node-feasible set, and let \(V(\bar x)=\sup\{\alpha^{\mathsf T}\bar x-\beta:(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal C_v\}\). An exact separation oracle returning no cut certifies \(V(\bar x)\le0\). A heuristic separator returning no cut certifies only that its search found none; it does not imply family-wide nonviolation, integrality, node optimality, or a pruning condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only a complete separator can turn “no cut found” into a family-wide nonviolation certificate; heuristic failure is merely a cut-round stopping event.
assumptions_latex: Every member of \(\mathcal C_v\) is valid for the node-feasible set.
The oracle reports whether its search was exact or heuristic.
The family has a fixed normalization so maximum violation is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{exact no-cut}\Rightarrow V(\bar x)\le0,\qquad \text{heuristic no-cut}\not\Rightarrow V(\bar x)\le0.

notation.meaning: Normalized supported family of cuts valid at node \(v\).
Maximum violation over the supported cut family.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Versus Heuristic Separation Outcomes
Node-Level Cut Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation and addition of valid inequalities at a branch-and-bound node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At node \(v\), let \(P_v\) be its current LP relaxation and let \(S_v\) be the feasible integer solutions compatible with the node restrictions. Solve the LP over \(P_v\) to obtain \(\bar x\). A separation oracle either returns no cut from its supported family or returns \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) satisfying \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) for every \(x\in S_v\) and \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}\bar x>\beta\). Add the inequality to \(P_v\), reoptimize, and repeat until the prescribed cut-round limit or separation stopping rule is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a search node, identify valid inequalities violated by the current LP solution, add them locally, and reoptimize before branching or pruning.
assumptions_latex: Every generated inequality is valid for the node-feasible integer set \(S_v\).
The separation and cut-round stopping rules are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each accepted cut removes the current relaxed point without removing any member of \(S_v\).

notation.meaning: Integer-feasible set compatible with node restrictions.

children.title: Global Cut Management
children.top_down_role: Retention, activation, and reuse of cuts across the search tree.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Cut Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity-preserving lifecycle management for cuts shared across the search tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a global pool \(G\) of inequalities valid for the original feasible set \(S\). A generated cut \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) may enter \(G\) only after its global validity for every \(x\in S\) is established. At each node, select a finite subset of eligible pool cuts using specified violation, efficacy, age, or density criteria; activate them in the node relaxation; and optionally retire inactive cuts from solver bases while retaining their validity metadata. Cuts valid only under node restrictions remain local and must not be propagated outside the corresponding subtree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Globally valid cuts may be shared and selectively activated throughout the tree; locally valid cuts must remain within their valid subtree.
assumptions_latex: Every pooled inequality carries a verified validity scope.
Cut activation and retirement preserve the underlying feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global-pool operations may alter relaxation strength and computational cost but cannot exclude any point of \(S\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the original mixed-integer model.

children.title: Tree–Cut Coordination
children.top_down_role: Interaction between tree-search decisions and relaxation strengthening.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree–Cut Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordination rule connecting cut generation, node bounds, pruning, and branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization search node \(v\), let \(P_v^{(0)}\supseteq P_v^{(1)}\supseteq\cdots\supseteq S_v\) be successive valid relaxations obtained by adding cuts, and let \(L_v^{(k)}=\inf\{f(x):x\in P_v^{(k)}\}\). Then \(L_v^{(k+1)}\ge L_v^{(k)}\). To use the strengthened relaxation's updated bound or optimizer for pruning, separation, or branching, the procedure must solve or validly bound that strengthened relaxation. A previously certified lower bound remains valid after further valid cuts, although it may be weaker. The node may be pruned when a certified relaxation bound is at least the incumbent value \(U\), or when infeasibility of a valid relaxation is certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid cuts can only strengthen the optimal node bound. Decisions attributed to the strengthened relaxation require an updated certified bound or solution, although an older certified lower bound remains safe but may be weaker.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization problem.
Every added cut is valid for the node-feasible set \(S_v\).
Every bound used for pruning is certified for a relaxation containing \(S_v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Valid cut addition cannot decrease the optimal node lower bound, and pruning remains sound when it uses any applicable certified lower bound at least \(U\).

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the relaxation after \(k\) cut rounds.

children.title: Cut-Integration Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Validity and performance limits at the tree-search interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Integration Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and bound-certification conditions beyond which integrating cuts can invalidate search conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_v\) be the feasible set under node \(v\). Adding \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) to the node relaxation preserves correctness only if the inequality is valid for every point of \(S_v\). Propagating the cut to an ancestor, sibling, or unrelated subtree is sound only when it is valid for the recipient feasible set. Pruning is sound only when the bound used is certified for a relaxation containing the recipient feasible set. A certified bound computed before valid cuts were installed remains valid after their installation, although it may be weaker; unsoundness arises when a bound is uncertified, belongs to an inapplicable node or relaxation, or is incorrectly attributed to an unsolved strengthened relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut integration is unsound when a cut leaves its validity scope or pruning relies on an uncertified or inapplicable bound; an older certified bound remains safe after valid cuts but may be weaker.
assumptions_latex: Search correctness requires preservation of every feasible solution in the recipient node.
Pruning decisions rely on certified bounds for relaxations containing the recipient feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A validity-scope violation or use of an uncertified or inapplicable bound crosses the sound cut-integration boundary.

children.title: NLP-Based Node Bounding
children.top_down_role: Direct convex nonlinear bounding at search nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: NLP-Based Node Bounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex nonlinear relaxation solved directly at each MINLP search node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex MINLP node \(v\), form \(X_v\) by retaining all convex constraints and node restrictions while relaxing the remaining integrality requirements. Solve \[L_v=\inf\{f(x):x\in X_v\}.\] If \(X_v\) is empty, prune the node. If a certified lower bound \(L_v\) satisfies \(L_v\ge U\), where \(U\) is the incumbent value, prune by bound. If an optimizer satisfies all integrality requirements, test it as an incumbent; otherwise choose a fractional discrete variable and branch. Any inexact NLP solve must return a certified lower bound before it is used for pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each node, solve the convex continuous relaxation directly, prune using certified bounds, and branch when the relaxed optimizer violates integrality.
assumptions_latex: The node relaxation is convex.
The objective and constraints admit globally valid feasibility and bound certificates.
The problem is minimized with incumbent value \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The computed \(L_v\) is a valid node lower bound and supports sound pruning when \(L_v\ge U\).

children.title: Outer-Approximation Tree-Search Interface
children.top_down_role: Tree search coupled to evolving linear outer approximations.

knowledge_statements.title: Outer-Approximation Tree-Search Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex MINLP tree search coupled to a dynamically strengthened linear relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider convex differentiable inequalities \(g_i(x)\le0\). Maintain a MILP relaxation containing node restrictions and supporting cuts \[g_i(z)+\nabla g_i(z)^{\mathsf T}(x-z)\le0\] generated at evaluated points \(z\). Solve the current node LP or MILP relaxation to obtain a lower bound and a candidate discrete assignment. For a new assignment, solve the associated convex NLP; use a feasible solution to update the incumbent and add its supporting cuts, or add a valid infeasibility-separating cut when the subproblem is infeasible. Reoptimize affected open nodes and stop when no node can improve the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tree search supplies discrete candidates and lower bounds, while convex NLP evaluations generate globally valid linearizations that strengthen the evolving linear relaxation.
assumptions_latex: Each \(g_i\) is convex and differentiable on a convex domain containing all evaluated points.
Generated optimality and infeasibility cuts are globally valid.
All pruning bounds are certified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The evolving outer approximation contains every feasible MINLP point and yields valid lower bounds for tree search.

notation.meaning: Point at which a supporting linearization is generated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective-Epigraph Supports in the OA Master
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-side linear outer approximation required when a convex nonlinear objective is represented in the tree master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and differentiable, and introduce \(\theta\) with \(\theta\ge f(x)\). For every evaluated point \(z\), the support \[\theta\ge f(z)+\nabla f(z)^{\mathsf T}(x-z)\] is valid for \(\operatorname{epi}(f)\). A node master containing these supports and globally valid outer linearizations of the nonlinear constraints therefore remains an outer relaxation of the epigraph formulation. Its objective value is a valid lower bound when it minimizes \(\theta\), or another certified objective underestimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex objective supports provide the epigraph underestimator needed for a linear outer-approximation master to return valid lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and differentiable on a convex domain containing the feasible region and evaluated points.
All constraint cuts in the master are globally valid.
The master minimizes \(\theta\) or another certified objective underestimator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta\ge f(z)+\nabla f(z)^{\mathsf T}(x-z)\text{ is valid for }\operatorname{epi}(f),\text{ and the master optimum is a lower bound}.

notation.meaning: Point at which an objective support is generated.

children.title: Conic Relaxation Variants

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-duality certificate for a linear conic node relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal conic node relaxation \[p_v=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax-b\in K,\ x\in B_v\},\] any dual-feasible certificate whose dual objective value is \(d_v\) satisfies \(d_v\le p_v\) by conic weak duality. Hence \(d_v\) is a valid node lower bound and \(d_v\ge U\) permits incumbent pruning. Strong duality, attainment, or a constraint qualification is needed only to conclude equality with \(p_v\), not for validity of a verified dual-feasible lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verified dual-cone feasible point certifies a node lower bound by weak duality; regularity is needed for equality, not for the lower-bound inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and the stated dual certificate is feasible for the correctly paired conic dual.
The dual objective value is evaluated rigorously.
\(U\) is a verified feasible incumbent value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_v\le p_v,\qquad d_v\ge U\Longrightarrow\text{node }v\text{ is prunable}.

notation.meaning: Closed convex cone defining the node relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Cone Node-Bound Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes certified conic pruning from solver statuses or approximate iterates that do not establish exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numerical conic solver status, an approximately dual-feasible iterate, or failure to find a primal point does not by itself certify a node lower bound or infeasibility. Bound pruning requires a verified dual-feasible value or another rigorous lower-bound certificate; infeasibility pruning requires a valid conic infeasibility certificate. Weak infeasibility or uncontrolled residuals can prevent either conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate conic solver output is not automatically a pruning certificate; exact or rigorously validated bound or infeasibility evidence is required.
assumptions_latex: Pruning is intended to preserve exact global-search correctness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{uncertified numerical status}\not\Rightarrow\text{valid node pruning}.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Certification Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical nonpolyhedral cone families used as continuous node relaxations after integrality is relaxed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A second-order-cone node relaxation uses constraints \(\|A_i x+b_i\|_2\le c_i^{\mathsf T}x+d_i\). A semidefinite node relaxation uses affine matrix constraints \(M_0+\sum_j x_jM_j\succeq0\). Finite products of nonnegative-orthant, second-order, and positive-semidefinite cones represent mixed conic variants. If the resulting continuous conic feasible region contains every mixed-integer feasible point of node \(v\), its certified optimum \(L_v\) is a valid minimization lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SOCP, SDP, and finite product-cone relaxations give valid node lower bounds whenever their continuous feasible regions contain every feasible point represented by the node.
assumptions_latex: The objective is minimized.
The conic relaxation contains every mixed-integer feasible point represented by node \(v\).
The reported conic optimum or lower bound is certified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_v\le\inf\{f(x):x\text{ is mixed-integer feasible in node }v\}.

notation.meaning: Certified conic-relaxation lower bound at node v.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order-Cone and Semidefinite Node Variants
Conic Relaxation Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node relaxations represented over closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conic node relaxation has the form \[L_v=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax-b\in K,\ x\in B_v\},\] where \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(B_v\) contains convex node restrictions after integrality is relaxed. Standard variants arise from \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\), a product of second-order cones, the positive-semidefinite cone, or products of these cones. If the original node-feasible set is contained in this conic feasible region, then \(L_v\) is a valid lower bound for minimization; strengthening the conic representation while retaining containment cannot decrease that lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic node bounds optimize over linear, second-order-cone, semidefinite, or product-cone relaxations that contain the node-feasible mixed-integer set.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The conic feasible region contains every feasible point of node \(v\).
The conic optimum or reported lower bound is certified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_v\) is a valid minimization lower bound at node \(v\).

children.title: Convex-Quadratic Relaxation Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Quadratic Relaxation Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex quadratic objective and constraint relaxations used for node bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex-quadratic node relaxation may be written as \[L_v=\inf\left\{\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_0x+c^{\mathsf T}x:q_i(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+a_i^{\mathsf T}x-b_i\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ x\in B_v\right\},\] with \(Q_i\succeq0\) and convex node domain \(B_v\). Variants include a convex quadratic objective with linear constraints, convex quadratic constraints with a linear objective, and their combination. When this feasible region contains all mixed-integer-feasible points compatible with node \(v\), its certified optimum \(L_v\) is a valid minimization lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex-quadratic node relaxations use positive-semidefinite quadratic objectives or constraints and yield valid bounds when they contain the node-feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_i\succeq0\) for every quadratic function used in the relaxation.
\(B_v\) is convex and contains the relaxed node-feasible domain.
The relaxation contains every mixed-integer-feasible point at node \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certified relaxation value \(L_v\) is a valid lower bound at node \(v\).

notation.meaning: Convex domain induced by node restrictions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity boundary for quadratic node relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+a^{\mathsf T}x-b\), global convexity is equivalent to \(\tfrac12(Q+Q^{\mathsf T})\succeq0\). If a minimized quadratic objective or a quadratic inequality written as \(q(x)\le0\) has an indefinite Hessian, the node problem is generally nonconvex, and a merely local solution does not certify a global lower bound. Certification then requires global optimization or replacement by a valid convex underestimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite quadratic generally destroys the convex-QP or convex-QCQP guarantee; a local optimum is not a certified node lower bound without global optimization or valid convexification.
assumptions_latex: Quadratic inequalities use the less-than-or-equal orientation.
Node pruning requires a globally valid minimization lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tfrac12(Q+Q^{\mathsf T})\not\succeq0\) removes the standard convex-quadratic certification guarantee.
